question: A commit that broke the build was pushed to `main` an hour ago, and teammates have pulled it since. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: `git reset --hard <sha>~1`, then `git push --force`
`git commit --amend` to rewrite the bad commit, then `git push --force`
`git revert <sha>`, then push the new commit
`git checkout <sha>~1`, then `git push`
explanation:
`git revert` creates a new commit that applies the inverse of the bad one, so history only moves forward and everyone can pull it normally.

Resetting or amending and then force-pushing rewrites commits other people already have: their next pull diverges, and work can be lost or the bad commit reintroduced. Checking out an old commit only moves your own `HEAD` (detached) and changes nothing on the remote.

question:
You're on `feature` and run `git merge main`. A file now contains:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout = 30
=======
timeout = 60
>>>>>>> main
```

Which statement is correct?
options: `timeout = 30` comes from `main`, because `HEAD` refers to the branch being merged in
`timeout = 30` is the version on `feature`; edit the file to the content you want, remove the markers, `git add` it, then `git commit` to finish the merge
Git has already chosen `timeout = 30`; the markers are only a note, so you can commit the file as it is
Run `git merge --continue` right away, and Git will keep both lines
explanation:
During a merge, `HEAD` is the branch you're on (`feature`), and the section after `=======` comes from the branch named after `>>>>>>>` (`main`). Git leaves the file conflicted until you write the final content yourself (one side, the other, or a combination), remove the markers and stage the file; `git commit` or `git merge --continue` then creates the merge commit.

`git merge --continue` refuses to run while files are still unmerged, and committing the markers would ship them in the file. Note that during a *rebase* the sides flip: `HEAD` is the branch you are rebasing onto.

question: You want to undo your last commit, which you haven't pushed, so that its changes are back in the staging area exactly as they were just before you ran `git commit`. Which command does that?
options: `git reset HEAD~1`
`git reset --hard HEAD~1`
`git reset --soft HEAD~1`
`git revert HEAD`
`git restore --staged .`
explanation:
`--soft` moves the branch pointer back one commit and leaves both the index and the working tree untouched, so the commit's changes are staged again.

Plain `git reset HEAD~1` uses `--mixed`, which also resets the index: the changes remain in your files but are no longer staged. `--hard` discards them. `git revert HEAD` keeps the commit and adds another one that undoes it, and `git restore --staged .` only unstages changes; it doesn't touch any commit.

question: `main` has gained new commits since you created your feature branch. On the feature branch you run `git rebase main` instead of `git merge main`. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The feature branch's commits are recreated with new hashes
The result is linear history without a merge commit
It is safe to do on a branch teammates have already pulled, without telling them
Conflicts may need resolving once per replayed commit, rather than once in total
The commits on `main` are rewritten too
explanation:
Rebasing replays each feature commit on top of `main`'s tip. Each replayed commit has a new parent, so it gets a new hash, and the history becomes a straight line. A conflict can stop the replay at every commit that touches the conflicting lines, whereas a merge resolves everything once in the merge commit. `main` is only read, never changed.

Because the feature commits are replaced, anyone who pulled the old ones now has diverged history. Rebase shared branches only by agreement, and push with `--force-with-lease`.

question: Branch `feat` was merged into `main` with merge commit `M`. A bug turned up, so someone ran `git revert -m 1 M` on `main`. Later you add a fix commit to `feat` and run `git merge feat` on `main` again. What does `main` contain afterwards?
options: Only the fix: the original feature changes stay reverted, because those commits are already part of `main`'s history; reverting the revert commit brings them back
All of `feat`'s changes, the original feature plus the fix, because a merge applies the whole branch again
Nothing new: Git reports `Already up to date` because `feat` was merged before
Git reports a conflict in every file the revert touched, and you pick the versions by hand
explanation:
A merge brings in only the changes from commits that aren't already reachable from `main`. The original feature commits are reachable through `M`, so Git treats them as merged, and the revert commit that undid their changes is in `main` as well. Only the new fix commit is new, so only the fix arrives, often leaving code that depends on the still-reverted feature.

The remedy is to revert the revert (`git revert <revert-sha>`) before or after merging again. `Already up to date` would only happen if `feat` had no new commits.
